1:
The problem is reconstructed first: Chrysostom says the charge cannot be grasped without the offence. Many at Corinth, having learnt that what enters does not defile and that idols can neither hurt nor help, made immoderate use of it, going in where the idols were and partaking of the tables. Both parties were injured: those who still feared idols joined in because they saw the more perfect do it, and ate as of a sacrifice, so the thing became a way to idolatry, while the perfect partook at the tables of demons. Henry describes the machinery: the heathen feasted on their sacrifices in the temple, sent portions to friends, and left the remainder to the priests, who sold it; and cites Athenæus that their feasts were all accounted sacred, so that eating unsacrificed meat at a private table was profane. Barnes and Ellicott give the same three ways the meat could reach a Christian, which Robertson counts as three questions Paul answers. Ellicott adds that so far as Paul’s own feelings went, we can scarcely doubt he would have eaten it. Gill supplies the church history, that the Jerusalem council had advised the Gentiles to abstain, which the Corinthians seem not to have known; Clarke a Jewish one, the long controversy between the Karaites, who held to the letter of scripture, and the Traditionists, who followed the elders, over benefit taken from heathen things.

The opening clause is read four ways. Lightfoot takes it as irony: all are agreed they know the liberty of the gospel well enough, and thereupon some run out into things not convenient. Robertson suspects a quotation from the Corinthians’ own letter, which Paul admits to be true. Calvin makes it a concession, granting everything they were prepared to demand so as to ask what such knowledge avails when it ruins the brethren. Wesley calls it a gentle reproof of self-conceit.

What the next sentence condemns is disputed with more heat. Calvin insists Paul condemns not knowledge itself but the haughtiness contracted from it, and refuses to let it teach scepticism or a counterfeit modesty, as though it were good to think ourselves ignorant of what we know; the beginning of true knowledge, he says, is an acquaintance with God which prostrates rather than elates, so that where pride is, there is ignorance of God. Barnes makes the fault a failure to use knowledge for others, a miserliness in knowledge as others are misers in wealth. Clarke turns it on the second commandment: a man who torments a neighbour’s tender conscience with his food does not love him as himself, and so knows nothing as he ought. Robertson makes it a point about depth rather than charity, citing Newton on gathering pebbles beside an unexplored ocean: the really learned man knows his ignorance of what lies beyond, shallow knowledge being like the depth of a mud hole, not a spring. Ellicott reports and rejects a rival sense for not yet, not in the infirmities of this mortal state, as introducing a thought the context does not answer.

The last clause turns on who is known. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley take the verb of divine approval, the man who loves God being approved as a genuine follower; Calvin agrees, glossing it as being reckoned among his sons, and adds that Paul erases the proud from the roll of the pious. Ellicott makes being known of God the source of knowing him, so that love and knowledge rise like water to the height of their source. Robertson alone leaves the referent open: the pronoun may point to the man who loves or to the God who is loved, and both are true, since God knows those that are his and those who know God are known of God; the perfect passive marks an abiding state of recognition, and none is acquainted with God who does not love him.
4:
How to render the first clause is disputed four ways. Lightfoot would have it that there is no idol in the world, taking the word as the lexicographers do, a likeness or image or shadow, and arguing that idols of wood and metal are in the world but that a representation of God is not, and cannot be. Clarke reports that rendering and sets it aside: the phrase was common in the Old Testament, where it means that these are not the true God but nothings and vanities. Calvin rejects a rival of his own, preferring the old an idol is nothing to Erasmus’s an idol has no existence, since the argument turns on there being but one God. Robertson reads it as saying no idol is anything in the world, notes that no copula is expressed, and reasons that the idol being a symbol, the god’s non-existence makes it a non-entity. Henry allows all three constructions, the original being elliptical, and notes that the Old Testament calls the heathen gods lying vanities, powerless to pollute what God has made.

Whose voice speaks here is a second question. Lightfoot holds that the apostle puts on the person of those who made no scruple about eating. Barnes reads the structure the same way: the admission runs through these three verses, the answer coming only in the next, where Paul shows the conclusion does not follow even on what he has granted. Calvin states it best: this is their excuse, and Paul sets it aside not as false, since it contains excellent doctrine, but as abused.

What the many gods and lords are divides them. Gill says they are gods by name and not by nature, angels and magistrates being so called in Scripture. Ellicott treats the sentence as a hypothesis with the verb emphatic, and grants it a footing, since the Old Testament speaks of gods and lords of another kind; the heathen many are deities, while the scriptural usage is only a casual way of speaking of angels and other servants of the one God. Robertson calls them so-called gods and takes a harder line: Paul denied their existence and held idol-worshippers really to worship demons. Calvin says they have the name but the reality is wanting, and divides them: those in heaven are the heavenly hosts, whose claim Moses overturns by showing they were made for our use, the sun our servant and the moon our handmaid; those on earth are men to whom divinity was ascribed, Pliny reporting that benefactors had their memory consecrated, mortal men afterwards exalted, and at length the Caesars.

The confession that answers them is read closely. Barnes argues that Father here is not the first person as against the second but a name for God as God, since Paul does not use the correlative Son at the one Lord; Gill offers that sense as one of two. Wesley guards the other side, that the one God excludes not the one Lord, as though he were an inferior deity, but only the idols. Robertson notes that Paul calls Jesus Lord here rather than God, though he uses that word of him elsewhere, and that the prepositions make him the agent in creation; Cyril of Jerusalem presses the title further: the Son is Lord of all, and nothing is excepted from his lordship, neither angels nor principalities nor powers nor any created thing. The one flat disagreement is over a preposition. Clarke renders the clause we for him, intelligent beings being created to manifest his glory, and Ellicott insists on for rather than in; Calvin weighs that sense, which makes God the end we devote our life to, and prefers to read it of our subsisting in God, preserved by the power that created us. Ellicott adds that the last clause is no repetition, physical creation being asserted first and our spiritual re-creation after.
7:
The admission is withdrawn as soon as granted. Barnes states the turn plainly: Paul had been rehearsing their own argument, and replies that though generally true it is not universally so, since some suppose an idol has a real existence. Calvin refutes in one word everything advanced in their name: it is not enough to know that what one does is right if one has no regard to a brother. They have a correct judgment before God, and alone in the world might eat what they pleased, but their actions are to be regulated not by their own knowledge only but by their brethren’s ignorance. Henry adds that weak Christians may hold even the plainest truths confusedly, and Gill limits the reference: Paul speaks not of heathens, who knew neither the one God nor the one Lord, but of Christians in some of whom that knowledge was wanting.

What the wanting knowledge amounted to divides them, and a variant stands behind the division. Ellicott reports that the manuscripts favour familiarity rather than conscience, and would attach the words up to this time to what precedes rather than to the eating, so that it describes converts who from a lifelong belief in the idol never grasped the non-existence of what it represents, and still take the meat as offered to some reality, even a demon. Robertson reads the same word and calls it the force of habit: they eat as of an idol sacrifice though they no longer believe in idols, the taint clinging in their minds. The others keep the received word and differ over its sense. Henry glosses it as a confused veneration retained for what they once worshipped. Barnes will not suppose they thought idols the only God, but may have taken them for intermediate beings whose favour was worth seeking. Gill has them grant that an idol is no deity while still fancying it can defile food. Clarke goes furthest: such a man treats the feast as a banquet giving fellowship with the idol.

How the conscience is defiled follows. Clarke says the man performs what he does as an act of religious worship and so contracts guilt through idolatry, and Wesley that he contracts guilt by doing it. Robertson locates the defilement elsewhere: not in partaking of polluted food, since food cannot pollute, but in doing what the unenlightened conscience does not allow — a man must act according to his conscience even when it is unenlightened, and knowledge breaks down as a guide where it is weak. Ellicott says only that the defilement arises from the weakness itself.

Whose argument the next verse states is a further question. Barnes takes it for the plea of those who wished to partake; Gill allows both, that it may be their argument or the apostle’s own sense; Calvin calls it another pretext of theirs and faults it for inferring the whole from a part, forgetting that love’s claims are included in the use of liberty. Ellicott makes it Paul’s own premise, the indifference of eating being why he can yield to another’s weakness, since if a vital relation to God were at stake yielding would be wrong. On the sense they agree. Gill glosses the verb as not bringing near or giving access to God, Clarke that eating gives no spiritual advantage and abstaining no loss, Wesley that both are merely indifferent, and Robertson that food gives no entrance to God for commendation or condemnation — a verse, he adds, that disposes at once of the pride of knowledge and the pride of prejudice. Calvin guards it: Paul speaks not of the stomach, since a man who has dined has the fuller one, but of righteousness, and not of every kind of eating, since excess and luxury displease God while sobriety pleases him. Ellicott notes that the closing clauses are inverted in the manuscripts the English version follows.
9:
The warning is put as the answer to their own plea. Barnes states it directly: grant all they say, that eating leaves a man neither better nor worse, and the governing principle is still that conduct injuring a brother settles the question. Ellicott turns the indifference into the reason for the rule: where a thing is right or wrong, that decides it; where it is indifferent, its effect on others must decide instead. Gill allows it to be either a reply to those who argued for eating or a limitation of the apostle’s own concession. Calvin says the liberty itself is left untouched and only its use moderated, and adds a limit of his own: regard is owed to the weak, but those who would tyrannically subject another’s liberty to their humour may be let alone, since men who catch at faults rather than stumble through infirmity need not be feared. Robertson dwells on the word rendered liberty, which covers a grant, an authority, a privilege, a right, and shades off until it becomes a battle cry for indulging appetite regardless of others.

The scene imagined is a meal in the temple itself, and it startles them. Clarke thinks it strange that a man professing to know the true God should enter such a place at all and stranger that a Christian should feast there, and concludes their boasted knowledge had little depth; the rabbinical writings, he notes, contain thin-spun theories permitting a man to enter and eat and even worship there provided his mind be towards the true God, and he names Lightfoot as his authority. Lightfoot supplies the material: the Talmudists dispute whether a man who adores an idol out of love or fear is guilty, and resolve it by intention — if he takes the image for God he is guilty, and if he takes the idol-temple for a synagogue his heart is towards God. Ellicott observes that some ate within the temple precincts, and that Paul lets that pass here, reserving his rebuke for a later chapter; Robertson agrees that such bravado is idolatrous in itself, Paul weighing here only its effect on the weak.

What the weak brother is built up to do is read with irony. Barnes and Clarke take the verb as confirming, settling a man in an opinion he had held doubtfully. Ellicott sharpens it: they had probably argued that their example would build others up, and Paul grants the word back to them — it will build him up, to do what being weak he cannot do without sin. Calvin describes the mechanism: the onlooker thinks himself excused by having someone to follow, while acting from an evil conscience. Robertson calls it defiance flung at a brother in place of loving consideration.

The last verse divides them twice over. Ellicott denies that it is a question, holding against the English version that it expands the preceding statement, that by thy knowledge the weak one perishes; he notes wide variation in the manuscripts. Calvin says plainly that he reads it interrogatively: is it reasonable that thy knowledge should occasion a brother’s ruin? On what the perishing means they divide again. Clarke will admit no quibble: a man for whom Christ died may perish everlastingly, since one who apostatises and dies in idolatry cannot go to heaven. Wesley agrees that Christ died even for them that perish, and adds the sharpest word in the chapter: for this brother the strong will not lose a meal’s meat, so far are they from dying for him. Barnes resists the inference: a real Christian is meant and ruin is the tendency, but a tendency may be arrested and need never issue in the event. Calvin turns from the question to the principle beneath it: whenever we act against conscience, even in a thing not evil in itself, we are on the high road to ruin.
12:
The blow is described before its object. Robertson notes that the verb means to smite with fist or staff, and that a conscience feels such a blow as a face feels a slap; Ellicott renders the clause as striking a blow upon their weak consciences. Barnes takes it of injuring, and explains that the weak are led further into error, believing the idol to be something and to be honoured, so that the conscience is more perverted and oppressed with guilt. Calvin refers back: a weak conscience is wounded when it is emboldened in evil, so as to rush further than the man himself thinks lawful. Gill locates the sin in the violated commandment: those bound to love one another as brethren must do nothing to prejudice another’s peace.

Why the injury reaches Christ is answered two ways. Barnes gives the union of members with head: they are so intimately joined to Christ that to offend them is to offend him, to injure the members is to injure the Head. Ellicott says the same in a sentence, that a member of that body which is his has been wounded, and Robertson supplies the proof from the words spoken to Saul, that in persecuting the disciples he was persecuting Christ himself. Calvin argues from the price paid: if the soul of every weak man is the price of Christ’s blood, he who for a small portion of meat hurries a redeemed brother back to death shows how contemptible that blood is in his eyes, and such contempt is an open insult. Clarke joins the two: the bad example sends to perdition a soul for whom Christ shed his blood and so far defeats the intention of his death — a further intimation, he adds, that a person for whom Christ died may perish.

The closing resolution is read carefully. Robertson observes that the first word should be rendered food rather than flesh, the second being flesh with direct reference to what was offered to idols, and notes the strong double negative: Paul would rather be a vegetarian than lead a weak brother into sin. Barnes glosses the closing phrase as meaning simply for ever, and calls the resolution noble and magnanimous, the very spirit of the self-denying Son of God. Calvin alone calls the expression hyperbolical, since a man who remains in common life can scarcely refrain from flesh his whole life long; Paul means that he would rather make no use of his liberty at all than be a stumbling-block, participation being lawful only when regulated by love. Gill reads it as a conclusion drawn for the writer and proposed for others to imitate.

All of them turn it on the reader. Calvin wishes it pondered by those who make everything subservient to their own advantage and cannot give up a hair’s breadth of their right, and asks that they attend not merely to what Paul teaches but to what he marks out by his own example, since if a man so greatly our superior subjected himself thus far to his brethren, none of us may refuse it. Wesley puts the challenge as two questions: who will follow this example, and what preacher or private Christian will abstain from a thing lawful in itself when it offends a weak brother? Clarke quotes Origen to the same effect, that brethren for whom Christ died often perish by many things in us, and the souls of those who perish by us will be required of us; and he draws the rule that the greater a man’s reputation for sanctity, the greater the mischief his example does if he turns aside, every man being bound so to walk as either to light or to lead his brother to heaven. Robertson closes on the same note: the questions of casuistry that arise now can be handled wisely only by Paul’s ideal of love.
